about: Every capability: the CLI command and the MCP tool that provide it, and the operation both of them run. `cli` is the command path without the binary; `mcp` is a tool name; `operation` is the function exported from packages/<package>/src/operations (or the core's) that both reach — a list when the command is several. `argv` and `args` are what the check adds to the command and the tool to get there — and what tells apart two rows of one command and one tool, `update --later` from `update --auto off` — `via` another row's operation a side passes through first, `expect` what the operation must receive from both sides, by parameter name (`null` for not given) — needed where another row runs the same operation through another command and another tool, so the two cannot be swapped unnoticed — and `unchecked` says why a row is not checked, instead of `operation`. Checked by test/parity.test.mjs in `pnpm verify` against both registries, read from the running product, and by running each row's command and tool with every operation replaced by a stand-in that records the call and its arguments; `pnpm verify:parity --strict`, also part of `pnpm verify`, refuses any pending row. How to add one: CONTRIBUTING.md, "Adding a capability". Design: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-25-cli-mcp-parity-design.md.

capabilities.reason: Which files may be attached: the folders they may come from, the person's own deny entries, and the built-in list. `comms_attach` with no change is this report.
A folder added widens what can be attached, so it is a change the person approves; the preview says where a link leads.
A folder taken away narrows what can be attached, and applies at once.
A deny entry added narrows what can be attached, and applies at once.
A deny entry taken away widens what can be attached, so it is a change the person approves; the built-in list cannot be removed.
Adding an organisation's profile — its Google client and Slack apps, beside what is here — is a change the person approves, bound to the profile's SHA-256 (design 2026-10-02 §D5).
Reading a profile again: a changed profile, a new source and serving other addresses are approved first; repairing drift, and turning other addresses off, apply at once (design 2026-10-02 §D8).
Forgetting a profile deletes the clients it made, with their secrets, and cannot be taken back: approved first, bound to the rows it removes (design 2026-10-02 §D8).

One change for every step: each registration registered again at the latest release with its own name, client, scope, launcher and pins, the runtimes that needs, and the global packages. `update --check` and `check: true` are `updateCheck`, the read both sides run instead, which asks nobody.
Not now: the daily update check's stop put off until local midnight, for the whole machine — a change the person approves, so an agent cannot clear the stop by itself (design 2026-09-28).
The daily update check on or off for this machine, in config.json: off is a loosening the person approves, on applies at once (design 2026-09-28).

Approving a change under the `confirm` change policy means a person at a terminal typing the code shown; a tool that approved would make `confirm` mean nothing (design §6.3). Under `chat` there is nothing to approve from a tool: the tool that prepared the change applies it when called again with the approval id, after the person's yes.
It runs the MCP server. A tool is a call into a server that is already running, so no tool can be the one that starts it.
`agentcomms mcp install` registers the core server; comms_server_install registers any channel's, and with `channel: "core"` is this command.
`agentcomms mcp prune` prunes the core's own runtimes; comms_server_prune takes the channel, and with `channel: "core"` is this command.
A change approval on both surfaces. The tool reads the client JSON from a path on this machine, so the file never passes through the conversation, and neither side returns the secret.

after.serverInstallChange: A sign-in `setup --mcp-client` handed off carries the client it was asked to register with, and `inbox add --finish` registers it once the mailbox is connected — through the change `mcp install` runs, approved the same way. gmail_inbox_finish does not: this server has no tool that registers anything, so it returns the registration as `pendingRegistration`, naming the core server's comms_server_install with `channel: "gmail"`, that client, `inbox` — the mailbox just connected — when the entry under that name serves another, `name: "gmail-<org>"` — a second entry of its own — when that entry serves another and is not being replaced, and `force` when `setup` was given `--replace-server` — the same change, from chat (design §5). Both decide by the same rule that the client already has it: an entry of ours under that name, at user scope, unpinned or pinned to this mailbox, whose runtime is there (`clientServesInbox`).

Both directions, for the send policy and the change policy. Tightening applies at once; loosening is a change approval on either surface (design §3). One row, since what was the loosening row now names the same command and tool.

capabilities.reason: The report `setup` starts from: the eligible client for the target mailbox, the clients and mailboxes there are, the MCP clients the server is registered with, the downloaded client files, and the one step to take next. With no --profile it changes nothing. The steps `setup` then takes are the rows that follow.

`setup --profile <file>` and gmail_setup profile add the organisation through core's orgAddChange first, under the separate --org-approval/orgApproval, then continue Gmail setup (design 2026-10-02 §D6).

capabilities.unchecked: `setup` registers the client only when `setupState` finds none, and in the drive `setupState` is a stand-in that finds nothing to compare, so `setup --client-json` never reaches the step there. It runs clientAddChange, as `client add` and gmail_client_add do: packages/gmail/test/account-changes.test.ts, "setup --client-json registers the client the same way client add does".
capabilities.reason: `setup --client-json <path>` registers the OAuth client through the change `client add` runs, under the name "desktop"; from chat that step is gmail_client_add.

`setup --inbox <name> [--email]` starts the sign-in `inbox add --start` starts; from chat that step is gmail_inbox_add, finished by gmail_inbox_finish. At a terminal, setup waits for the browser itself.
`setup --mcp-client <client>` registers the server as `mcp install` does; from chat that step is the core server's comms_server_install with `channel: "gmail"` (design §5).

`workspace add <name>` with no client id chooses the organisation profile's read app, or its send app for `mode: "send"`; an explicit client id and port keep the own-app path. Send is approved before sign-in; read starts at once.

Changes nothing and starts nothing: returns the steps for a move to send. For a profile account those steps are the move to the profile's send app, which `slack_mode_set` (`workspace mode <name> send`) performs after approval and Slack consent; for an own-app account they are the existing manifest/app-update steps.

Changes nothing and starts nothing: returns the steps for a move to read. For a profile account those steps are the move to the profile's read app, which `slack_mode_set` (`workspace mode <name> read`) performs at once, followed by Slack consent; for an own-app account they are the existing manifest/removal/reauth procedure.

`workspace mode <name> send|read` moves a profile account between the organisation's apps (`send` needs approval; `read` starts at once); an own-app account keeps the existing app-update/removal instructions.

Choosing which file on this Mac an agent may read is the person's decision, and the first read of WhatsApp's folder is the moment macOS asks that person for permission, which a server cannot answer. Refused to an agent at the command line too.
The other half of `add`: it forgets the account, the person's chat lists for it and its index. The person's step, refused to an agent at the command line too.

Which chats an agent may see is the person's choice, in both directions: a tool would let an agent widen what it sees. Kept outside `config.json`, where no loosening of it could be judged, and refused to an agent at the command line too.
The other side of `allow`: an agent neither widens nor narrows what later sessions see. The person's list, refused to an agent at the command line too.
It undoes `allow` and `deny`, which are the person's; emptying an allow list shows every chat again, which an agent must not be able to do.
